title: The ECI offers relief to a section of deleted electors but SIR’s flaws remain
content_html:
Following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI) in some States that had undergone the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), mostly in Phases 1 and 2, some 74 lakh names were added onto the electoral rolls. This meant that the electorate in those 13 States, that had shrunk from 49.61 crore to 45.22 crore after the SIR, has now gone up to 45.96 crore. The ECI has extended the SSR to States and UTs in Phase 3. As before, it requires no proof of citizenship or mapping to older rolls, and insists on personal notice before any deletion other than of the dead. It also directs Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to cross-verify deletions personally wherever they exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors. Draft deletions in Phase 3 of the SIR averaged 17%, and reached 32.8% in Delhi. The ECI also offered another opportunity to electors deleted by the SIR in the seven States and UTs where it is still underway, such as Delhi and Maharashtra, to return to the rolls. Electors who did not return their forms can do so now, explaining the delay, and those who moved within the State can return through the enumeration form with proof of their new address. EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.

These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

title: Europe must be part of any settlement on the Ukraine war
content_html:
The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War. In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.

That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military. Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow. European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

title: India’s minerals policy needs to move to material security
author: Rohan Gupta
content_html:
One can auction a lithium block in a day. Turning what lies beneath it into a resource that Indian battery manufacturers can use is an entirely different story. Bridging that gap between a resource and a usable supply will shape the next phase of India’s critical minerals policy.

In the last two years, the government moved the sector up on their policy agenda. The National Critical Mineral Mission was allocated ₹34,300 crore for a seven-year program covering exploration, mining and processing of critical minerals and materials. The amended mining law enables the government to auction blocks of 24 critical minerals; more blocks are expected to be auctioned before 2031.

title: What protections do workers in India have in case of layoffs?
author: Nivedita Varadarajan
content_html:
Layoffs have become an increasingly prominent feature of the employment landscape. The growing adoption of artificial intelligence and the significant investments companies are making in AI infrastructure have added to concerns about job security and the future of employment. Against this backdrop, as India marks the first anniversary of the implementation of its four Labour Codes on November 21, we examine the question of severance pay and the wider social security framework for workers who lose their jobs.  What protections do workers in India have in case of layoffs? K.R. Shyam Sundar and Rahul Charkha discuss the question in a conversation moderated by Nivedita Varadarajan. Edited excerpts:

K. R. Shyam Sundar is former Professor, Human Resource Management area at Xavier School of Management in Jamshedpur; Rahul Charkha is partner at Economic Laws Practice

title: M.S. Dhoni: A diplomat, a wit, and a man of few words
author: K.C. Vijaya Kumar
content_html:
A splendid cricketing journey recently wound to a close as M.S. Dhoni moved into the realm of mentorship. Just as tributes about this magnificent player and leader pour in, it is also time to recall the communication traits of Dhoni, the enigmatic personality.

A packed sporting calendar often means that the intersection between celebrity athletes and the media stays restricted to press conferences steeped in platitudes. The one-to-one interview is now a rarity, and glimpses into how a player thinks are gleaned from general media interactions.

title: Letters to the Editor — November 20, 2026
content_html:
Poisonous air

The poison we inhale every day rarely creates the urgency it deserves. Perhaps we have become too accustomed to grey skies and the annual advice to stay indoors. People need to understand both the immediate harm of polluted air and the damage that builds over years. A little fear, grounded in facts, is necessary to disturb this complacency. But warnings must come with practical protection and visible action. What does “stay indoors” mean to a street vendor, a construction worker or a child living beside a busy road? Clean air cannot depend on the ability to buy an air purifier.

title: The changing dynamic of nationalism in India
author: D.V. Kumar
content_html:
Many social science scholars have argued that nationalist and ethnic feelings would become weaker in the context of developed capitalism and modernity. However, we now know that nationalism continues to remain an implacable force. There is no dearth of literature about what nationalism means and how one makes sense of it. Here, we will look at two forms of nationalism and contextualise it by looking at the changing dynamic of nationalism in India.

Broadly speaking, one can refer to two kinds of nationalisms — civic and ethnic nationalism. The former is based on shared respect for values of liberty, equality, justice and fraternity and an unshakeable faith in the constitutional framework. It is inclusive, progressive, liberating and democratic. It seeks to bring together people who are otherwise extremely diverse in terms of their religions, social practices, languages, food habits, cultures etc. It takes special care to ensure that the marginalised and historically oppressed groups are accommodated within the nationalist framework. It also gives space to every identity to nurture itself unhindered.

On the contrary, ethnic nationalism focuses on essentialising and privileging a single identity via religion, language, or ethnicity and is therefore exclusionary, regressive, destructive and undemocratic. It poses physical and epistemic danger to those identities which do not fall within the dominant understanding of what nationalism is. Hitler clearly espoused ethnic nationalism (the superiority of Germanic Aryan race) which led to unspeakable atrocities being committed against Jews in Nazi-era Germany. 

The nationalism that grew in India during the freedom struggle was largely civic in nature. It was an inclusive, liberating, and democratic project. There was a strong conviction that what was being sought was worth fighting for and morally and ethically justified. There was almost a touch of romance; one could not but fall in love with the ideals of justice, equality, freedom and secularism, which were the guiding principles of the nationalism that was experienced during the freedom struggle. It was an open invitation to explore. In this endeavour, science was to be a partner.

When the Constitution, which was a product of reasoned debates and contestations, came into existence, it unleashed enormous democratising possibilities. Its incorporation of fundamental rights and freedoms was a paradigmatic shift in a society which had and still has some of the most oppressive structures in the world such as the caste system. A democratic Constitution could have emerged only in the context of democratic nationalism.

title: Many imperatives: On India’s Asia diplomacy
content_html:
Each year, the summits of the 11-member Association of South-East Asian Nations mark an important moment on the diplomatic calendar: India is able to interact with all of its partners in the Indo-Pacific and engage global powers at the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s talks with Indo-Pacific players focused on a future shaped “not by competition, but by cooperation”. This year, the summit in Manila hosted by the Philippines had many other imperatives. These were the first ASEAN summits since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and Iran’s Hormuz blockade and strikes on Gulf countries that have upended energy and trade across South and South East Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world during the EAS was aimed as much at leaders from the U.S., Russia and China as it was for the region. The visit had a bilateral context — the Philippines and India have intensified ties considerably in the past year, since the visit of President Bongbong Marcos to Delhi in August 2025, including the upgradation of the Strategic Partnership, maritime exchanges and negotiations over the supply of more Indian-made Brahmos missile battery systems to the Philippines. This year, after months of concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump’s lack of interest in the Quad grouping, the U.S. decided to host a summit of U.S.-India-Australia-Japan Quad leaders on the side-lines of the ASEAN summits, the first time the summit has been held in a non-Quad country.

Given the stakes, there were several outcomes from all the three summits that PM Modi attended back-to-back on Tuesday — the ASEAN India Summit launched a new cooperation on disaster management, and the East Asia Summit focused on countering cyber-crime. PM Modi’s announcement that India would give all ASEAN citizens free tourist visas is expected to increase people-to-people interactions and trade. At the Quad summit, President Trump made a number of announcements including the launch of a Quad Business leaders forum, to be held in Mumbai next year, and the first Quad naval exercises with patrol aircraft. However, the outcomes in Manila paled in significance to the anticipation over Mr. Trump’s next stop in Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Conference (APEC), with an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping planned on Thursday. New Delhi must watch the outcomes of that summit among the “global superpowers” much more closely.

title: Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
content_html:
New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.

For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.
